articles.sourceTitle: Memdoor: A team of 5 Qwen3.8-27B models beats Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard
articles.title: memdoor/examples/workflows/team-solve at main · guregodevo/memdoor · GitHub
articles.text:
Five small models solve a programming problem together: a planner, two
ideators, a solver and a manager, plus a repair worker. Each starts from a
fresh context and talks only through files on disk. A script that runs the
samples decides success, not a model. It is the method of
GVS5H (Lee, 2026), written as a
Memdoor workflow: eight YAML files, no code, no model
named.

The authors' harness rebuilt on the same model, Qwen3.8-27B, with their
prompts, loop and 128K reply cap. The first ten problems of their
LiveCodeBench Hard list, five passes each, graded on every hidden test with
their corrected grader:

Fable 5, one call

10 / 10

mean
9.8
9.6
8.0

The authors' two columns are the regraded result files in their repository,
the numbers in their paper. Our column is
bench/results/parity-5pass/: all 50 runs,
each with every request and reply, the program, the grader's output and the
cost. A run took a median of 40 minutes and $0.39; the 50 cost $35.79.
What this does and does not show:

Ten problems, five passes, not the authors' 100. On a sample this small,
9.8 and 9.6 are the same number. The claim is parity with their harness, not
a gain on it.
The contests date from spring 2025 and the model may have seen them in
training. Contamination cannot be ruled out, for any column.
Fable 5's column is one call per problem, from the authors' files. It was
not run in this harness.
On these ten, the authors' own five-pass data put Fable 5 at 80 and their
harness at 96; the workflow's 98 reproduces that gap. Across their full 100,
harness and Fable are 92.4 and 90.4 (their patched_verdicts.json).
The loop sees only the public samples; the score is the hidden tests.
The model ran on OpenRouter, not a local machine.
The one lost problem: the manager invented a wrong counterexample and the
team rewrote a correct program. Twice elsewhere a correct program was
overwritten and then recovered. Both gaps are the authors' loop, kept as is.

The parity check (every request byte for byte against their code), the hosts,
the changes it took and the first run's findings are in NOTES.md.
The same result, on one page: memdoor.ai/docs/team-solve.

curl -fsSL https://memdoor.ai/install.sh | bash
memdoor connect openrouter        # or anthropic, openai, gemini, chatgpt
# or no key: memdoor connect local   (Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM, LM Studio; Ollama needs a 32K window, not its 4K default)
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/guregodevo/memdoor

mkdir -p ~/.memdoor/workflows
cp -r memdoor/examples/workflows/team-solve ~/.memdoor/workflows/
mkdir my-problem && cd my-problem
cp -r ../memdoor/examples/workflows/team-solve/sample/* .    # task.md + tests/1.in … 5.out
memdoor workflow run team-solve --wait   # exit 0 when every sample passes

For your own problem, replace task.md and put paired tests/N.in /
tests/N.out beside it. The program is solution.py, read from stdin,
compared to the samples with diff; it needs Python 3 and bash. /workflow
in memdoor tui draws the run live.
The steps name no model: whatever /model is pinned to answers, a local one
included (how to connect one).
To change a role, change its prompt in steps/.

plan ──┬── ideate-a ──┬── solve ── test ── review ── repair ── verify
└── ideate-b ──┘

Every agent prompt says "fresh context, read the files, do not rely on chat".
The paper credits that ledger discipline for the gain. Each step is one YAML
file in steps/, in the format of mario,
the engine underneath; requires: is the DAG.

articles.sourceTitle: The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks
articles.title: The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks
articles.text:
One of my pet peeves with the web development community is that so many of the decisions we make are vibes-based. Frameworks are “blazing fast,” tools will “supercharge” your development, the right abstraction will benefit both you and your users (DX and UX all in one!). All of this breathless boasting is usually offered with zero evidence. Alex Russell has called this “frontend’s lost decade”, Baldur Bjarnason has called programming a pop culture, and I’ve tried to counter this trend in my blog with facts and benchmarks (at my best, anyway).
For a long time it seemed like our community’s allergy to evidence was driven by the desire for greater DX. In other words, devs just liked the way it felt to type JSX in React, and the arguments promoting React or related tools (“the virtual DOM is fast!”) were largely post-hoc rationalizations to justify those initial gut feelings. (Jonathan Haidt would likely agree with this assessment.)
But in the agentic era, when developers are no longer typing code by hand and are thus less constrained by DX, I still see vibes ruling the day (and not just in the sense of “vibe-coding”). Frontends are rewritten because some framework or another is “better for agents.” (Did anyone think to ask the agents?) The resulting code is “faster,” the agents make “fewer mistakes,” etc. Once again, these claims are often made without evidence. Whenever I read one of these accounts, I think to myself, “Where are the benchmarks?”
Well I got curious, so I wrote a benchmark. The structure of this benchmark is pretty straightforward:

Design a small but non-trivial Pokémon app using the PokéAPI (those who have followed my work will be unsurprised)
Instruct agents to build the app with a particular JavaScript framework/meta-framework (e.g. Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, etc.)
Test the output against a spec conformance suite (to avoid agent cheating)
Evaluate the results in terms of development time, tokens spent, lines of code, and performance and accessibility scores in Lighthouse

The app is fairly simple: you’ve got a list of Pokémon with their types, moves, and data from various games. You can search, filter, etc.:

I should start off with some caveats: this is not a perfect experiment. This app represents only one holotype – it’s a relatively content-based site with little interactivity, closer to a Wikipedia than a Figma, GMail, etc. That said, I had to choose some app to build, and this one is at least easy to understand at a high level, and relatively straightforward to spec out and test.
To try to even the playing field, I had each framework/meta-framework use the official MCP or skills for that tool. I wanted to avoid accusations of “this framework is not well-represented in the training data, that’s why we built our MCP, we expect people to use it,” etc. I also didn’t over-specify the exact architecture to use (e.g. SSR vs CSR), nor did I specify that the app should be as performant as possible. I simply gave the spec to Opus 5.5 with high effort and told it to use the latest version of the given framework. Each agent ran in a sandbox and without any knowledge that it would be tested in Lighthouse on performance and accessibility, although it was given the conformance test suite.
Note I also didn’t mandate any CSS methodology, except to avoid using Tailwind, Bootstrap, or any other component framework, and to design based on a set of spec tokens to enforce some visual consistency. I didn’t want to make this test all about CSS, but instead about JS frameworks, CSR vs SSR, SPAs vs MPAs, etc. The resulting app is tested against a conformance suite based on the accessibility tree rather than the raw DOM to avoid mandating any particular HTML structure – one framework uses web components which rely on shadow DOM, so this was required.
One thing I learned from this experiment is that everything I’m measuring is very stochastic. LLMs are random-word generators, so sometimes you get a low dice-roll and an agent goes off on some weird tangent wasting a bunch of tokens, through no fault of the framework or its tools. Lighthouse itself can give inconsistent results as well: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) may decide that one image is the “largest” element, then pick another one on the next run. It’s hard to have a perfectly fair experiment, but running multiple iterations did help, and I’ve tried to be honest about the variance.
With all that throat-clearing out of the way, let’s get to the results.
Results
I’m going to break this down by multiple dimensions: cost to build, quality, and maintainability. For each framework/meta-framework, I took the median of 5 runs: in other words, I built the same app 5 times in the same framework. (Yes, this is the kind of zany thing you can do with coding agents these days.)
The exception was Angular, which failed to create a working app twice, so I took 3 iterations instead. (This is explained below.)

Note that this quotes the API prices directly from Claude Code and doesn’t actually represent how much money I spent. I’m on a Max plan, so this was just part of my overall $100/month.
Note also the variance: React Router’s median is roughly $1 worse than that of Hono+htmx, but the cheapest version of React Router ($2.82) is still cheaper than the most expensive version of Hono+htmx ($3.19). However some reliable patterns do emerge.
Most clearly, SvelteKit, Gracile+Lit, and Angular are more expensive to build than the other frameworks. For SvelteKit, this may be due to the fact that the agents read the SvelteKit v3 migration guide in every run, likely because it’s too new to be in Opus 5.5’s training data. Similarly for Gracile, the agents didn’t know the framework very well and either cloned the Gracile repo or read its compiled source from node_modules. For Angular it seems to be a function of the total code size (see below).
I should also mention that not every agent made use of an MCP/skill/Claude Code plugin, nor did every framework have one:

Click to see AI tool usage

For example, TanStack Start’s agent only discovered its skill files in 2/5 runs (they’re shipped in the node_modules of the project). For Nuxt, the MCP was never used by the agents. For Next.js, agents only read the skill file in 1/5 runs and the AGENTS.md in 2/5 runs. This is a wide range of results, which points back to the stochastic nature of LLMs. I still consider this a valid experiment, though, because I doubt many vibe-coders are shouting at their agents in all-caps to use the MCP (and plenty are probably skipping it entirely).
Also, if you’re wondering how I came up with Hono+htmx: essentially, I wanted htmx represented somehow, and Hono seemed like a fine pairing (i.e. as a JavaScript alternative to Rails/Django/etc.). As for Gracile+Lit, I wanted web components represented via their standard-bearer framework (Lit), and was only aware of Gracile as a meta-framework. If there are better candidates, then those would be great for a follow-up experiment.
For “Vanilla,” note that the agent was told to use “vanilla JavaScript or TypeScript with Vite, without a UI framework.” Surprisingly, this underperforms several frameworks, which seems to demonstrate that having some framework can be better than nothing (or better than raw Vite, anyway). Vite was chosen because it undergirds many frameworks and represents fairly standard and agnostic JavaScript infrastructure.

Quality
Of course, because I think that outcomes matter, I also tested the agents with Lighthouse. As software developers, I think it’s important that we not only build things cheaply but also performantly and accessibly.
I should first note two caveats about my benchmark:

The Pokémon app is small and doesn’t represent a large, complex real-world application.
Lighthouse and the Core Web Vitals in general are biased against SPAs, so the MPA frameworks are almost guaranteed to win on metrics like Total Blocking Time (TBT), JavaScript bytes, etc. I considered adding some in-app performance metrics but backed off because it added complexity and variability to the benchmark, and these would be metrics I invented as opposed to industry standards.

For simplicity’s sake, I’m only reporting the scores for the home page. There are other pages, but they all score fairly similarly or they have wild swings in metrics like LCP, so it just complicates things to include them.

AI agent swarms in Minecraft fail to build civilization, drown in bureaucracy
articles.title: AI agent swarms unleashed in Minecraft to ‘build a thriving civilization’ — 50-agent teams fail after falling into paralyzing bureaucracy
articles.text:
Follow us

Add us as a preferred source on Google

Subscribe to our newsletter

AI researchers at ycombinator and Olam Labs recently tested AI agent swarms in gaming scenarios. Minecraft and its various game modes were the sandboxes where 100s of agents were unleashed to work together or as adversaries. The idea seems to be that the in-game collaborations and conflicts would provide insight into real-world headline-grabbing cases with AI agents involved.This study might help us see what happened, good and bad, in recent AI swarm cases, and thus developers of this technology can improve it. The blog mentions two contrasting cases, which were the thousand-agent swarms that “recently obliterated hundreds of open mathematical problems,” and the “extremely dangerous” OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. This research is built on prior work and frameworks, specifically repos like Mindcraft and scripting tools in Mineflayer.Multi-agent dynamics in MinecraftThe first AI swarm testing plan was a simple collaborative one. During this test phase, the researchers tasked 50 agents with building a thriving civilization in three hours. It seems to have tested 50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents here, but not any Claude agents.Probably the most interesting insight from this ‘Civ50’ test was that the 50-strong colony never really thrived. After the first night saw zombies take out a large number of agents (but with little penalty) it was noted that “many ambitious initial tasks were abandoned.”From then on, the colonists cautiously survived, and there was a tendency toward bureaucracy. As an example, “four agents spent 11 minutes appointing a ‘sole fertilizer operator’ for a single piece of bone meal on a single wheat block.” The researchers say this AI agent swarm behavior “felt similar to patterns seen while working with coding agents.”

(Image credit: ycombinator)Next up, the researchers decided to put AI agent swarms into conflict. First they tested them in Bed Wars, which is a kind of team PvP capture the base, while defending yours game mode. The setup was 10 GPT‑6.1 Sol vs. 10 Claude Opus 5.5 agents.“GPT agents came up with much more aggressive and elaborate strategies,” noted the researchers. Claude was more defensive. It was also interesting to observe contrasts in how the teams handled problems. “A tool bug stopped block-breaking. GPT diagnosed it and shared workarounds; several Claudes concluded breaking was impossible.”Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.Finally, the agents were tested in Mindustry, a kind of light RTS combat game with tower defense mode in Minecraft. “The GPTs won 6-1 against the Claudes in the 7 games,” which was a great result for the OpenAI-created agents. Researchers concluded that GPTs acted more like a hive, while Claudes had a single leader but a democratic-style decision process. In Mindustry, the former was the foundation for a more consistently winning strategy.These swarms are open sourced so you can run your own, if you are interested in tweaking and testing. The source blog post ends with some open questions that you can check hands-on, offering some directions for investigative probing. For example, it is suggested that comparing different mixes of models and varying sizes of agent swarms in Minecraft might raise worthwhile conclusions.

Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.

Mark Tyson is a news editor at Tom's Hardware. He enjoys covering the full breadth of PC tech; from business and semiconductor design to products approaching the edge of reason.

GPT-5.6 Sol can beat Factorio on peaceful mode
articles.title: GPT-5.6 Sol can beat Factorio
articles.text:
GPT-5.6 Sol can beat Factorio

·
Oct 31, 2026

Edit: Woah, this took off! If you want more details you can subscribe at the bottom of the post or on YouTube. I’m working on a more detailed highlights/commentary post and video.
Previously: We got Claude Code playing Factorio, Towards beating Factorio autonomously, and Faketorio: an agent testbed
I got GPT-5.6 Sol, running in Codex with low thinking level, to complete a peaceful (i.e. no biters) Factorio run in 13.5 hours of game time:

A timelapse of the full run is available on YouTube.
Similar to my previous post, this run used a game manager to allow Sol/Codex to interact with the game via a small library (though in this run it was Python rather than Bash). The library allows the model to play the game programmatically while enforcing the same restrictions that human players face when using the GUI (e.g. reach of the player, fog of war).
Observing the run was fascinating: Sol exceeded my expectations in some areas while also showing clear weaknesses in others. I have the entire run recorded and am working on a commentary video, but in the meantime here’s a small timelapsed segment showing some parts of the factory:

Besides the screencast, my run manager also captured production statistics throughout the game. Here’s a chart of total resource production, annotated with science research milestones:

I had planned to terminate the run after blue science research, but Sol’s surprising effectiveness convinced me to keep it going. Unfortunately, the scaling issues I thought would occur in the blue science stage appeared later and slowed Sol’s relative progress significantly.
The rocket launch was only achieved through significant ‘manual’ effort on Sol’s part as it papered over its late-game failures to connect certain production systems by repeatedly ferrying supplies between areas of the factory.
Still, I was pleased with the improvement over previous attempts with GPT-5.5 which suffered from the model’s failures to use transport belts at all.
I’m optimistic about autonomous Factorio play as a medium for building intuition about the nature of model capabilities. In many ways playing Factorio is analogous to programming but with the benefit of being much more legible to casual observers, making it convenient for grounding discussion of model behaviors.
I look forward to testing other models and thinking levels, as well as non-peaceful runs. Stay tuned!
